system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2137-08-02 19:59:00 to 2137-08-05 16:26:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for a scheduled bronchoscopy with balloon dilation due to recurrent tracheobronchial stenosis from relapsing polychondritis and SMAD4 syndrome. Post-procedure, he reported left-sided chest pain consistent with prior experiences, which resolved without intervention. He remained stable throughout the admission, with no respiratory distress or signs of infection. His white blood cell count was elevated but attributed to chronic inflammation and steroid use. The chest X-ray showed stable cardiomegaly and clear lungs. He was discharged home the following morning in stable condition with instructions to follow up with interventional pulmonology and primary care, continuing his baseline medications including methotrexate and prednisone.
problems: Other specified diseases of upper respiratory tract
Other specified congenital malformation syndromes, not elsewhere classified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I understand you've been having trouble breathing for about three weeks now. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse. I’ve had this thick yellow mucus coming from my trach, and I just can’t catch my breath like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned in the ER that this feels similar to when you had your last bronchoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Last time, after they cleared out the mucus, I felt so much better. I couldn’t get in for a scheduled bronch, so I came here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve reviewed your history — you have relapsing polychondritis and SMAD4 syndrome, which cause your airway to narrow over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I get monthly bronchoscopies to keep it open. But missing one really threw me off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled interventional pulmonology to do a bronchoscopy with balloon dilation tomorrow. That should help open up your airway and clear the mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel much. Afterward, we may give you some pain medicine if needed. We did check your labs — your white blood cell count is high, but that’s common for you due to your condition and steroid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. No fever this time, so it’s probably not an infection, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we think. Your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or fluid. So we believe this is mostly mucus buildup from the stenosis. We’ll confirm more after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds right. I just want to breathe normally again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. You just got back from your bronchoscopy. Everything went well — they dilated your trachea and both main bronchi. They removed a lot of thick mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little groggy, but my chest feels looser already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We also sent a sample of the washings from your airway to check for infection. We saw some gram-negative rods, which means we’ll start you on antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics? But I don’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: True, but because of your trach and frequent procedures, we don’t want to take chances. The culture grew Klebsiella oxytoca, which is treatable. You’ll take cefpodoxime for six days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually, especially since it’s sensitive to the antibiotic. It’s likely from your own airway flora. We’re just being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my breathing — should it keep improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, over the next day or two. We’ll monitor your oxygen levels. You desaturated a bit when walking earlier, so we’ll keep an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel short of breath just going to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ordering a CT scan tomorrow to make sure there’s nothing else going on, like a small area of infection or collapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan came back. Good news — your airway looks stable, no new blockages or clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the desatting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan showed some subtle inflammation in your lungs, but nothing acute. It’s likely related to chronic changes from your condition. Your oxygen improved with rest, so we think you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re actually improving. Your white count is coming down — it was 14, now it’s 10.7. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on your usual — prednisone, methotrexate, folic acid, famotidine, calcium, vitamin D. We held losartan because your blood pressure was a bit low, but your PCP will restart it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the inhaler?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding Symbicort twice daily to help with airway inflammation and keep things open. It works with your other treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll use it. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep doing this well, probably tomorrow morning. We’ll make sure you can walk without desatting too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interventional pulmonology will call you to schedule your next bronchoscopy. And please see your primary care doctor to review your meds, especially losartan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made great progress. Your breathing is better, and your labs are improving. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep caring for your trach as usual, take all your meds — especially the cefpodoxime for the full six days. Finish the Symbicort as prescribed. And watch for fever, increased mucus, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel like I’m getting blocked up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call interventional pulmonology. Don’t wait too long. And if you can’t reach them, come back to the ER. You know your body best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — should I restart losartan on my own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, please wait for your PCP to tell you. We held it because your BP was lower in the hospital, but they’ll decide when it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your care team will send instructions to your home. Someone from pulmonology should call within two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I don’t hear, I’ll call them directly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Don’t hesitate. We want to keep you stable and out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for progressive dyspnea and productive cough over three weeks, consistent with mucus accumulation due to recurrent tracheal stenosis from relapsing polychondritis and SMAD4 syndrome. He had missed a scheduled bronchoscopy and presented with increased yellow tracheal secretions. He underwent flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of the trachea and both main bronchi, which relieved his symptoms. Bronchial washings grew Klebsiella oxytoca, prompting a seven-day course of cefpodoxime. A CT chest showed stable airway stenosis and no acute findings despite transient desaturation with ambulation. His white blood cell count improved from 14.0 to 10.7, and he was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to complete antibiotics, continue baseline medications, and follow up with interventional pulmonology and primary care.
